column3: No, thank you. That's fine as it is.
column6: A complete, polite no.

column2: Sí, también un agua, por favor.
column3: Yes, a water as well, please.
column6: Adds a second thing without repeating the first.

column3: Nothing else, thank you.
column6: The shortest way to close the order.

column2: Sí, pero algo pequeño, por favor.
column3: Yes, but something small, please.
column6: Says yes and sets the size.

column3: How much is it all together?
column6: For the whole order rather than one item.

column3: How much is the coffee?
column6: Asks about one thing before ordering it.

column3: How much is the biscuit?
column6: For the extra rather than the drink.

column3: Sorry, how much is it?
column6: When you missed the number the first time.

column3: That's very kind, thank you.
column6: Warmer than gracias on its own.

column3: Thank you, see you later.
column6: The everyday close.

column3: Everything was perfect, thank you.
column6: Says the food or the service was good.

column3: It's very good, thank you.
column6: A compliment on the way out.

column2: ¿Giro a la izquierda o a la derecha?
column3: Do I turn left or right?
column6: Offers both, so the answer cannot be ambiguous.

column3: Straight on as far as the square?
column6: Reads back the first half.

column3: And after the pharmacy?
column6: Asks for the next step only.

column2: ¿Es la primera calle o la segunda?
column3: Is it the first street or the second?
column6: The detail that is most often missed.

column3: And where do I turn?
column6: When you have the direction but not the place.

column3: Do I go past the bank?
column6: Names a landmark to confirm the route.

column3: How many minutes is it?
column6: Asks for a number instead of a feeling.

column3: Can I walk there?
column6: The question behind the question.

column3: Is it better to go by bus?
column6: Asks for a recommendation, not just a distance.

column3: That is very kind of you.
column6: Formal and warm.

column3: Thank you, now I know where it is.
column6: Confirms the help worked.

column3: Perfect, that's it. Thank you.
column6: Short, when you are already moving.

column2: Muchas gracias, es una gran ayuda.
column3: Thank you very much, that is a great help.
column6: For someone who went out of their way.

column2: Uso la talla treinta y ocho.
column3: I take a size thirty-eight.
column6: When you know the local number.

column3: I don't know my size here.
column6: Sizes differ by country, and saying so is normal.

column2: Creo que es la talla pequeña.
column3: I think it's the small size.
column6: Hedged, when you are guessing.

column3: Where can I try the shirt on?
column6: Asks for the fitting room without naming it.

column3: Can I try both on?
column6: For when you cannot choose yet.

column3: Can I try this jacket on?
column6: Names the item you are holding.

column2: Quiero probar la talla más grande.
column3: I want to try the bigger size.
column6: A statement, after the first one did not fit.

column3: I'll take this shirt.
column6: The plain decision.

column3: I'll go with the blue one.
column6: Chooses between two.

column3: I'd rather think about it a bit more.
column6: A polite no that leaves the door open.

column3: How much is this shirt?
column6: Before you commit to trying it on.

column3: How much are the two together?
column6: For two items at once.

column3: Sorry, how much is it?
column6: When you missed the price the first time.

column3: Can I pay by card here?
column6: Worth asking before you get to the till.

column3: Good afternoon, I have a reservation.
column6: Opens the whole exchange in one line.

column3: Yes, under the name López.
column6: The detail they actually need.

column2: Tengo una reserva para esta noche.
column3: I have a reservation for tonight.
column6: Adds how long, unprompted.

column3: I have no reservation. Do you have any rooms?
column6: The other case, and it happens.

column3: What is included in the price?
column6: Open, so you hear about things you would not ask for.

column3: Does breakfast cost extra?
column6: The question behind the question.

column3: Does the room have a bathroom?
column6: Cheap rooms sometimes do not.

column3: What time does breakfast start?
column6: The one you will need tomorrow morning.

column3: What time does breakfast finish?
column6: More useful than when it starts.

column3: What time do I have to leave?
column6: Check-out, without needing the word for it.

column3: Does the restaurant open at eight?
column6: Proposes a time and lets them correct it.

column3: What time does the bar close?
column6: For the evening.

column3: Can I arrive later?
column6: When your train gets in at midnight.

column3: Is there a bar near the hotel?
column6: Outside the hotel rather than in it.

column3: What floor is my room on?
column6: Ask before you carry the bags up.

column3: Where is the entrance?
column6: For a hotel with more than one door.

column2: ¿Tienes planes para el fin de semana?
column3: Do you have plans for the weekend?
column6: Opens without committing you to anything.

column3: Shall we do something tomorrow?
column6: Direct, and easy to say yes to.

column3: Are you free this afternoon?
column6: Checks first, suggests after.

column3: What shall we do tomorrow?
column6: Assumes the plan and asks only what.

column3: Do you want to go for a drink?
column6: The lowest-commitment suggestion there is.

column2: Podemos ir al parque por la tarde.
column3: We could go to the park in the afternoon.
column6: A suggestion with a time attached.

column3: Shall we go to the new restaurant?
column6: Names somewhere specific.

column3: Do you fancy a coffee?
column6: Apetecer is the natural verb for this in Spain.

column3: What time shall we meet?
column6: The plain question.

column3: Shall we meet at seven?
column6: Proposes a time rather than asking for one.

column3: Could it be later?
column6: Moves the time without rejecting the plan.

column3: Where shall we meet?
column6: The other half of the arrangement.

column3: Perfect, see you on Sunday.
column6: Says the day back, which is what fixes it.

column2: Muy bien, entonces a las ocho.
column3: All right, eight o’clock then.
column6: Says the time back.

column3: OK, I'll see you there.
column6: Casual, and very Spanish.

column3: Great, see you tomorrow.
column6: Warm, for a plan you are pleased about.

column3: Good afternoon, how are things?
column6: Time of day plus an opener, in four words.

column3: Hi, I'm Luis. And you?
column6: Gives your name and hands the turn straight back.

column3: Good evening, sir.
column6: Formal, and for after dark.

column3: Hi, how is everything going?
column6: Warmer than ¿cómo estás? with someone you know.

column3: Right, see you later.
column6: Bueno is what signals you are leaving.

column3: See you tomorrow.
column6: When you know when.

column3: Until next time.
column6: When you do not.

column3: Have a good day, and see you soon.
column6: Warm without being long.

column1: # ── Routine: the detail that makes it yours ───────────────────────────────────

column2: Normalmente no tengo mucho tiempo por la mañana.
column3: I usually don't have much time in the morning.
column6: A circumstance rather than an action.

column2: Voy al trabajo en metro y llego a las nueve.
column3: I go to work by metro and arrive at nine.
column6: How you travel, and when you land.

column2: Salgo pronto y llego a la escuela antes de las ocho.
column3: I leave early and get to the school before eight.
column6: A different destination, the same shape.

column3: For three days now.
column6: The bare answer, with desde hace.

column2: Desde el fin de semana pasado.
column3: Since last weekend.
column6: Anchors it to a day rather than a count.

column3: It started yesterday morning.
column6: Says when it began instead of how long.

column3: Yes, a slight temperature.
column6: Yes, with the degree.

column3: No, I'm not taking any medication.
column6: The question they always ask.

column3: I've been sleeping badly since Monday.
column6: Answers about sleep with a start date.

column2: Como bien, pero estoy muy cansado.
column3: I'm eating well, but I'm very tired.
column6: Rules one thing out and offers another.

column2: Como bien, pero estoy muy cansada.
column3: I'm eating well, but I'm very tired.
column6: Rules one thing out and offers another.

column2: De acuerdo, voy a descansar dos días.
column3: All right, I'll rest for two days.
column6: Accepts, and says how much.

column2: Muy bien, tomo una pastilla por la noche.
column3: All right, I'll take a tablet at night.
column6: Repeats the instruction back.

column3: Understood. And if I am not better?
column6: Accepts, then asks the obvious next question.

column2: Gracias. Voy a beber mucha agua.
column3: Thank you. I'll drink plenty of water.
column6: Names the advice you are going to follow.

column3: I have three meetings this week.
column6: How many, over what period.

column2: Hablo con los clientes por teléfono.
column3: I talk to the customers on the phone.
column6: For work that is meetings by another name.

column2: Los lunes tenemos una reunión de equipo.
column3: On Mondays we have a team meeting.
column6: A regular one, anchored to a day.

column2: Fue un día difícil, pero bueno.
column3: It was a hard day, but a good one.
column6: Two verdicts at once, which is usually the truth.

column2: Hoy termino pronto y estoy contento.
column3: I finish early today and I'm happy about it.
column6: The reason and the feeling together.

column2: Hoy termino pronto y estoy contenta.
column3: I finish early today and I'm happy about it.
column6: The reason and the feeling together.

column2: Llego a casa cansado, pero tranquilo.
column3: I get home tired, but calm.
column6: Tired is not the same as unhappy.

column3: There is a shop very close by.
column6: The thing people ask about first.

column2: La parada de autobús está delante de casa.
column3: The bus stop is right in front of the house.
column6: Names how close, not just that it exists.

column2: No hay tiendas cerca. Es un problema.
column3: There are no shops nearby. It is a problem.
column6: What is missing is as useful as what is there.

column2: Cerca de casa hay un parque muy grande.
column3: There is a very big park near the house.
column6: Puts the place first, which is natural in Spanish.

column3: I live very well here.
column6: About the living, not the flat.

column2: Es un poco pequeño, pero me gusta.
column3: It's a bit small, but I like it.
column6: The honest verdict most people give.

column2: No me gusta la calle, es muy ruidosa.
column3: I don't like the street, it's very noisy.
column6: Negative, and says exactly what about.

column2: Quiero cambiar de casa el año que viene.
column3: I want to move house next year.
column6: A feeling expressed as a plan.

column2: ¿A qué hora sale el próximo tren?
column3: What time does the next train leave?
column6: The question that starts every journey.

column3: When does the next bus leave?
column6: Cuándo, when you do not need the exact hour.

column3: Is there a later one?
column6: When the next one is too soon.

column2: ¿El tren llega antes de las diez?
column3: Does the train arrive before ten?
column6: About the arrival, which is what you actually need.

column3: Return, please.
column6: The two words that answer the standard question.

column3: One ticket, one way.
column6: How many and which fare at once.

column3: Two tickets for tomorrow.
column6: Adds the day, which they will ask for next.

column3: How much is a return?
column6: Asks the price before choosing.

column3: Which platform does it leave from?
column6: The last thing between you and the train.

column3: Where is platform three?
column6: Once you know the number.

column3: Is this the right stop?
column6: For a bus, where there is no platform.

column2: ¿Sale de aquí o del otro andén?
column3: Does it leave from here or the other platform?
column6: Offers both, so the answer cannot be vague.

column3: How much is a kilo?
column6: The straightforward form.

column3: How much are the lemons?
column6: A cuánto están is what you will actually hear.

column3: How much for two kilos?
column6: For the amount you want, not the unit.

column3: And how much is half a kilo?
column6: Half a kilo is the usual market amount.

column3: Make it a kilo rather than half.
column6: Mejor is how you change an order politely.

column2: Perdón, cambio de idea. Dos, por favor.
column3: Sorry, I have changed my mind. Two, please.
column6: Says plainly that you are changing it.

column3: I would like some bread as well, please.
column6: Adds rather than changes.

column3: No, just the oranges.
column6: Takes something back off the counter.

column3: Can I pay in cash?
column6: Small stalls often prefer it.

column3: Here's ten euros.
column6: Says the amount as you hand it over.

column2: Gracias, hasta la semana que viene.
column3: Thank you, see you next week.
column6: For a stall you will come back to.

column3: That's all right. Thank you very much.
column6: Confirms the change was right on the way out.

column2: Trabaja en una tienda del centro.
column3: She works in a shop in the centre.
column6: Where, when the job has no short name.

column2: Es estudiante y trabaja por las tardes.
column3: He is a student and works in the afternoons.
column6: For someone doing both.

column2: No trabaja ahora, busca algo nuevo.
column3: She is not working at the moment, she is looking for something new.
column6: Honest, and very common.

column2: Es camarero en un restaurante del centro.
column3: He is a waiter in a restaurant in the centre.
column6: Job and place in one line.

column3: There are four of us at home.
column6: The size of the household, in three words.

column3: My brother is thirty.
column6: Ages use tener, not ser.

column2: Tengo dos hijos, de seis y de nueve años.
column3: I have two children, aged six and nine.
column6: Two ages without repeating años twice.

column2: Mis padres viven en otra ciudad.
column3: My parents live in another city.
column6: Where, rather than who or how old.
